\chapter{Grandparents, and the Married Pair}
\label{ch:te-grandparents}
\hlchaptermodality{45}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name a grandfather, a grandmother, a husband and a wife in Telugu.}

Complete TE-C45-wife and say all four words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[tāta]{\te{తాత} (tāta) — grandfather}

\label{lesson:TE-C45-grandfather}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{rāyi} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{తాత}}
\textbf{\te{తాత}} (\emph{tāta}) — \textquotedblleft{}grandfather\textquotedblright{}.

It has the same small, repeatable shape as the \emph{nānna} and \emph{amma} you met in the family lesson. Sanskrit carries a \emph{tāta} too, meaning 'father' or simply 'dear one'; Telugu moved the word up a generation. Children use it for any kindly old man, not only their own grandfather.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of four family words. Three follow, and each reuses the ones before.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tāta}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item it after \emph{rāyi}, so the two sit together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{తాత} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}grandfather\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ammamma]{\te{అమ్మమ్మ} (ammamma) — grandmother, the mother's mother}

\label{lesson:TE-C45-grandmother}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{tāta} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{అమ్మమ్మ}}
\textbf{\te{అమ్మమ్మ}} (\emph{ammamma}) — \textquotedblleft{}grandmother\textquotedblright{}, and specifically your mother's mother.

Say it slowly and you can hear what it is made of: \emph{amma} twice over, mother of mother. Telugu keeps the two grandmothers apart, and the father's mother is \emph{nāyanamma}, assembled the same way on \emph{nāyana}, 'father'. Nothing here is borrowed; every piece came from the family lesson.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two of four, and a word you could have decoded before you were taught it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ammamma}
  \item it once more, slowly, hearing the two halves
  \item it after \emph{tāta}, so the two sit together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{అమ్మమ్మ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}grandmother\textquotedblright{}, the mother's mother.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bharta]{\te{భర్త} (bharta) — husband}

\label{lesson:TE-C45-husband}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{ammamma} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{భర్త}}
\textbf{\te{భర్త}} (\emph{bharta}) — \textquotedblleft{}husband\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit, and it opens cleanly: the root \emph{bhṛ}, 'to bear, to carry, to support', plus the ending that names the one who does it. So the word says 'the one who supports'. That root is old enough to have relatives far outside India — Latin \emph{fero}, 'I carry', and English \emph{bear} both continue it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three of four. The last word comes from the very same root.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bharta}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item it after \emph{ammamma}, so the two sit together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{భర్త} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}husband\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bhārya]{\te{భార్య} (bhārya) — wife}

\label{lesson:TE-C45-wife}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{bharta} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{భార్య}}
\textbf{\te{భార్య}} (\emph{bhārya}) — \textquotedblleft{}wife\textquotedblright{}.

The same root \emph{bhṛ} as the last word, with a different ending: 'she who is to be supported'. Two words, one root, and between them a picture of the household as Sanskrit's grammarians framed it rather than as anyone lives in it now. That is worth hearing plainly, because the shape of the pair is the reason it is easy to remember.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
That closes the run: grandfather, grandmother, husband, wife.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bhārya}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item it after \emph{bharta}, and name the root they share
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{భార్య} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}wife\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
